new_statements.quote: 2b. Stress Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI kala, snake, for instance. [preceding 2a Tone text:] ... differ in tone pattern, while there is tonal difference in BONGO and 'BELI in the material collected by Santandrea and Tucker; ... [fn.] Not even in 'BELI, where both investigators used the same informant at different times. But it was also discovered that in both BONGO and 'BELI the informants themselves would give different pronunciations on different days.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no Beli record and our earlier reading (Stirtz 2014, Beli Grammar Book 2013) found no stress statement at all, so this is the first stress statement located that covers 'Beli, but only at the level of the Bongo-Bagirmi group, with the one concrete example from Bagirmi (a different language). The item is borrow-only on archive.org (access-restricted-item true; download = not reachable by automated download); the text was reconstructed verbatim from overlapping search-inside snippets, so page number and any 'Beli-specific footnote to the stress paragraph could not be checked.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages (whose data set explicitly includes 'Beli, from Santandrea's MS sketch and Tucker's own fieldwork with the same informant): stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, obligatorily so when the second syllable has a 'semi-mute' (reduced) vowel; stress can shift to the second syllable when the first syllable contains a central vowel (only example given is Bagirmi kala 'snake', from Stevenson). Vowel-quality-sensitive initial stress in a tone language (three tone levels plus rising/falling are recorded for the group in 2a).
new_statements.exceptions: stress heard on the second syllable when the first syllable has a central vowel (Bagirmi kala 'snake'); no 'Beli-specific example
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (Persson & Persson 1991) describes Mödö = Jur Modo (ISO bex), a sister language of 'Beli (ISO blm) in the Beli-Modo subgroup, not 'Beli. Work 1 (Tucker & Bryan 1966) treats the whole Bongo-Bagirmi group in one chapter; its 'Beli data come from Santandrea's manuscript sketch and Tucker's own elicitation with the same informant (variety not named). The previously checked Stirtz 2014 is on the Wulu dialect of 'Beli.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another, but they are not on the same footing. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (group-level Bongo-Bagirmi paragraph, reconstructed from search snippets) gives initial stress on disyllables with vowel-quality conditions, but its only example is Bagirmi, and it is unclear from the snippets whether the 'Beli data contributed to the claim. The dedicated modern descriptions of 'Beli already checked (Stirtz 2014 SIL e-WP, the 2013 SIL-South Sudan Grammar Book and dictionary) describe three level tones on CV syllables and say nothing about stress, and Persson 1991 is about Modo, not Beli, and is also silent on stress. A catalog entry for Beli would have to be flagged as resting on a 1966 group-level remark rather than a Beli-specific statement.

sources.note: Nothing: no section or sentence on stress/accent/prominence (0 hits; only 'acute accent' as a rejected orthographic device). Sec. 3 (p. 6): syllables almost all CV, no consonant or vowel sequences, no contrastive length. Sec. 4 (p. 7): three underlying level tones (H, M, L) plus contours; 'The syllable is the tone-bearing unit.' Secs 6.x: extensive tonal morphophonology and grammatical tone. Wulu dialect.
